stem.presentation: A 75-year-old woman with non-small cell lung cancer after chemotherapy and radiation, COPD and hypertension presented for the third time with dyspnea and hemoptysis. At her most recent discharge she had improved on an aggressive COPD regimen and went home on standing inhalers and a 5-day course of cefpodoxime and azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia. One day later, after a large meal and a walk to the bathroom, she became much more dyspneic. She denied chest pain, palpitations or diaphoresis; cough had improved but rusty sputum persisted, and left ankle edema and pain had improved with an arthritis pill from her pulmonologist. In the ED WBC was 15,000, Cr 1.7 (1.3 at discharge), troponin 0.14 without ECG changes, and BNP 3309 (2522 earlier); CXR showed increased right hilar and left lower lobe infiltrates and a left pleural effusion. She received bronchodilators, methylprednisolone, vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, aspirin and fluids ahead of a planned CTA, and was sent to the floor.

stem.presentation: A 52-year-old man, a dentist with multiple sclerosis and a strong family history of premature CAD but no personal cardiac history, developed rapid-onset chest heaviness and a general sense of feeling funny just after finishing his usual wheelchair-based morning exercise. The discomfort radiated to his neck, jaw and left ear and later down his left arm. It eased somewhat on its own but returned by the time he reached work; two sublingual nitroglycerin tablets from the office emergency kit brought near complete relief. His PCP referred him to the ED, where the ECG was unremarkable and the first set of cardiac enzymes was negative. Based on his history he was given aspirin and metoprolol and started on a heparin infusion, and he remained pain free thereafter. He reported a viral syndrome with chills two weeks earlier and denied exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, palpitations or syncope.
